summary: Raspberry Pi Pico soldered flat to a 2-layer PCB with 9 Kailh hot-swap sockets for MX switches, directly wired to 9 GPIOs. Two-part 3D printed case: the top doubles as the switch plate, the bottom tray holds the PCB on standoffs. Four M3 screws into heat-set inserts.
architecture: USB micro-B on the Pico -> VBUS 5V -> Pico VSYS (no external regulator)
9 switches, one per GPIO (GP2-GP10) to GND, internal pull-ups, no diodes or matrix
Firmware: KMK on CircuitPython 10.3.1, firmware/code.py, written from the routed board by distinta pcb
Stack (top down): keycaps, switches clipped into 1.5 mm printed plate, PCB 5.0 mm below plate top, sockets under PCB, tray
assembly: Order the PCB (Gerbers in pcb/) and the two case prints (fab/top.stl and fab/bottom.stl, PETG, 0.2 mm layers, top printed plate-down).
Solder the 9 hot-swap sockets onto the back of the PCB while it is bare and lies flat, face down.
Turn it face up (it rests level on its sockets) and solder the Pico flat onto the PCB by its castellated edges, USB end flush with the right edge.

Flash the Pico: hold BOOTSEL, plug it in, copy CircuitPython 10.3.1 for the Pico onto the RPI-RP2 drive, then KMK's kmk folder onto CIRCUITPY (firmware/README.md links the two the firmware is tested with). Unplug. (Later, the small hole in the lid reaches BOOTSEL.)
Press the 4 M3 heat-set inserts into the top shell's bosses with a soldering iron at about 220 °C, then set the top on the PCB.
Clip the 9 switches into the plate, pressing each until its two pins seat in its socket; keep the PCB flat on the bench so the sockets are backed.
Set it all in the tray and fasten with the 4 M3 screws from below.
Press a keycap onto each switch.

Plug the USB cable into the Pico and copy firmware/code.py onto CIRCUITPY. It reads each key on the GPIO the board wires it to, K1 GP10, K2 GP7, K3 GP4, K4 GP9, K5 GP6, K6 GP3, K7 GP8, K8 GP5, K9 GP2, and the keys type 1 to 9 until you put your shortcuts in its keymap (firmware/README.md says how). Keys are numbered from the bottom left, row by row (K1 to K3 along the bottom, K7 to K9 along the top, the USB end on the right); the labels under the keys say the same.
Test: each key should type its number, or the shortcut you gave it. If one doesn't, check its socket joint first.
estimates: bootselFromUsbEndMm, bootselAcrossMm, ledFromUsbEndMm, ledAcrossMm: measured on Raspberry Pi's pinout drawing (to about 0.3 mm), not dimensioned in the Pico datasheet; check against your board before printing the top

Kailh socket body outline, the no-track area under each socket (pipeline/pcb/footprints.ts KAILH.body): traced off Kailh's drawing (+-0.05 mm), which dimensions only its length and widths; the socket's holes and pads are sourced (pipeline/pcb/fixtures/footprint-refs.json)
usbOvermoldWidthMm, usbOvermoldHeightMm: a typical micro-B cable's moulding (the sourced cable's page gives no size)
sw spec pinWidthMm, pinThicknessMm, centrePostLengthMm: from MX-style switch drawings, used only by the figure; pinLengthMm 3.3 and the 4 mm centre hole are the MX standard
